result:
Solutions 1 and 3 give the same function and I accept both, though the upper bound in Solution 1 rests on a cited independence-number result I did not prove. Solution 2 is wrong.

**Solution 1.** The construction is valid. Take D = {±1, …, ±q} with q = ⌊p/(r+1)⌋ and S its complement in Z_p \ {0}. A clique in Cay(Z_p, S) is a set whose cyclic gaps are all at least q+1, so its size is at most ⌊p/(q+1)⌋. Since q+1 > p/(r+1), this is at most r, so the graph is K_{r+1}-free.

The matching upper bound uses the claim that a symmetric set D of size 2k in Z_p gives an independent set of size at least ⌊p/(k+1)⌋. I did not prove this, but it is consistent with every case I checked: r=1, r=p−1, and small cases such as p=5, 7, 11, 13 with r=2 (symmetric sum-free sets) and p=7 with r=3.

The second form of the answer agrees with the first. Since (p+1)/2 is an integer, ⌊(p+1)/2 − (p+1)/(r+1)⌋ = (p+1)/2 − ⌈(p+1)/(r+1)⌉, and ⌈(p+1)/(r+1)⌉ = ⌊p/(r+1)⌋ + 1. So 2⌊(r−1)(p+1)/(2(r+1))⌋ = p−1−2⌊p/(r+1)⌋.

**Solution 2.** Its answer is p−1−2⌈(p−1)/(2r)⌉. For r=2 this is about p/2, but triangle-free circulants on Z_p have at most about p/3 connection elements (symmetric sum-free sets). For example, with p=7 and r=2 the formula gives 6−2·2 = 2 only by coincidence of rounding, but for p=11 it gives 10−2·3 = 4, and for larger p it overshoots. The solution itself notes this contradiction and then guesses anyway, so the answer is not established. Reject.

**Solution 3.** The formula is p−1−2·max(1, ⌊(p−1)/(r+1)⌋). The quantities ⌊p/(r+1)⌋ and ⌊(p−1)/(r+1)⌋ differ only when (r+1) divides p, which for 1 ≤ r ≤ p−1 means r+1 = p. In that case ⌊p/(r+1)⌋ = 1, and the max(1, ·) in Solution 3 also gives 1, so both give p−3. The two formulas therefore agree for all r, and Solution 3 matches Solution 1.

VERDICT 1: ACCEPT
VERDICT 2: REJECT
VERDICT 3: ACCEPT
